content: Stavudine is a nucleoside analogue of thymidine that undergoes phosphorylation by cellular kinases to form its active metabolite, stavudine triphosphate. This active metabolite inhibits the function of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) by competing with the natural substrate, thymidine triphosphate, with an inhibition constant (Ki) ranging from 0.0083 to 0.032 µM. Additionally, stavudine triphosphate causes termination of the viral DNA chain when incorporated into the viral DNA. It also inhibits cellular DNA polymerases β and γ, significantly impairing mitochondrial DNA synthesis. The antiviral activity of stavudine has been evaluated in cell culture using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, monocytic cells, and lymphoblastoid cell lines. The concentration required to inhibit HIV-1 replication by 50% (EC50) ranged from 0.009 to 4 µM against both laboratory and clinical isolates of HIV-1. In cell culture, stavudine demonstrated additive to antagonistic activity when combined with zidovudine. However, when combined with abacavir, didanosine, tenofovir, or zalcitabine, stavudine exhibited additive to synergistic anti-HIV-1 activity. Ribavirin, at concentrations of 9–45 µM, reduced the anti-HIV-1 activity of stavudine by 2.5to 5-fold. It is important to note that the correlation between cell culture susceptibility of HIV-1 to stavudine and its ability to inhibit HIV-1 replication in humans has not been established. HIV-1 isolates with reduced susceptibility to stavudine have been identified both in cell culture and in patients treated with stavudine. Phenotypic analysis of HIV-1 isolates from 61 patients who received stavudine monotherapy for 6–29 months revealed that post-therapy isolates from four patients exhibited EC50 values that were 7to 16-fold higher than the baseline susceptibility of pre-treatment isolates. Among these, isolates from one patient contained the zidovudine-resistance-associated mutations T215Y and K219E, while isolates from another patient harbored the multiple-nucleoside-resistance-associated mutation Q151M. No mutations in the reverse transcriptase gene were detected in the isolates from the other two patients. The genetic mechanisms underlying changes in stavudine susceptibility remain unidentified. Cross-resistance among HIV-1 reverse transcriptase inhibitors has been observed. Prolonged treatment with stavudine has been shown to select for or maintain thymidine analogue mutations (TAMs), including M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y/F, and K219Q/E, which are associated with resistance to zidovudine. HIV-1 isolates containing one or more TAMs demonstrated reduced susceptibility to stavudine in cell culture. These TAMs occur at similar frequencies in patients treated with stavudine or zidovudine. Clinically, these findings suggest that stavudine should not be used in the presence of thymidine analogue mutations.
